h1: Everything that counts as SEO work
metaTitle: What Does SEO Include? The Full Work List
metaDescription: What does SEO include? More than forty distinct activities across five areas. Here's the full list, grouped, with how often each one needs doing.
answer: SEO includes about forty-five recurring activities across five areas: technical fixes, content and on-page work, links and digital PR, local signals, and measurement. Roughly a quarter are one-time setup, the rest repeat weekly, monthly or quarterly. A scope that lists fewer than twenty of them is missing a whole discipline.
takeaways: Five areas, roughly forty-five activities. Most retainers cover three areas well and two badly.
**Cadence is the thing to check, not the list.** Everyone can list 'technical SEO'. Ask how often each item actually gets done.
About twelve activities are genuinely one-time. Paying a monthly fee for them forever is how retainers quietly go stale.
Use this page as a scope template or a job description. Delete the rows that don't apply to you and make the agency price what's left.

sections.h2: Five areas, and why the cadence column matters more than the list
body: Every agency can recite the categories. Technical, content, off-page, local, reporting. The list is not the useful part — it's on every pitch deck in India and it tells you nothing about whether the work happens.

What separates a real scope from a nice deck is frequency. "We do technical SEO" can mean a full crawl every quarter with a fix queue, or one audit in month one that nobody opens again. Same words, wildly different invoice.

So each table below carries a cadence label. **Once** means setup work that shouldn't recur unless something changes. **Weekly** and **monthly** mean it belongs in a standing calendar. **Quarterly** means it's cheap to skip and expensive to have skipped.
This is the plumbing. It rarely wins you a ranking on its own, and it caps everything else when it's broken. On a site older than three years it's usually where the first genuine gains hide.

callout.title: Scope this properly
callout.body: Technical work eats 20–30% of hours in month one and drops to around 10% after. If a proposal keeps billing month-one technical hours in month eight, ask what's being crawled that changed.

body: The largest line in almost every retainer, and the one most often reduced to "four blogs a month". Writing is one of eleven things here. The other ten are what decide whether the writing earns anything.

sections.h2: Links and digital PR: eight activities
body: The area with the widest quality gap between agencies, because the cheap version and the expensive version look identical on a report. Both produce a number of new referring domains. Only one of them survives a spam update.

callout.title: The question that separates the field
callout.body: "Where do the links come from?" A real answer names sites and methods. "Our network" or "high-DA blogs" means bought placements on a private network, and Google's link spam policies have been eating those for years. See [what a link building programme should cost](/cost/link-building-cost).

sections.h2: Local SEO: seven activities, if you have an address
body: Skip this section entirely if you're a pure-play SaaS or a national e-commerce brand with no physical presence. If you have clinics, stores, branches or a service area, this is often the fastest-returning work on the whole list — and it barely touches your website.

table.caption: Local SEO activities for businesses with a physical or service-area presence.
head: Activity
What it means in practice
Cadence
rows: Correct primary category, services, hours, attributes, photos
Fresh images and updates — the profile is a live surface, not a listing
A repeatable ask built into your delivery, plus replies to every review
Consistent name, address and phone across directories and aggregators
One real page per branch with unique content, not a list of eleven addresses
Sponsorships, associations, local press, community listings
Map pack position measured across a geographic grid, not one point

body: The area clients cut first and regret last. Without the first row on this table, nothing else on this page can be proved to have worked.

head: Activity

GA4 events, forms, calls and CRM lead source actually firing

What moved, why, and what happens next month. Two pages, not twenty

Checking whether a drop was you, Google, or seasonality

sections.h2: What's genuinely one-time — and how to turn this into a scope
body: Twelve of the activities above are setup: the first crawl, robots and sitemap, the redirect audit, schema per template, the JS rendering check, hreflang, keyword mapping, the intent audit, the backlink audit, Business Profile setup, location pages, and analytics and baseline setup. They should be finished inside the first quarter and never billed as recurring work again.

Everything else repeats. That's the honest reason SEO is sold as a retainer rather than a project — not because agencies like recurring revenue, though they do, but because roughly thirty-three of these forty-five items have no finish line. The [retainer versus project comparison](/compare/retainer-vs-project) goes deeper on where that line should sit.

To use this as a scope: delete the rows that don't apply, put a name against every remaining row, and ask what happens to the cadence if hours run short in a busy month. The answer to that last question is where most retainers quietly fail.

callout.title: What a ₹75,000 retainer covers
callout.body: Roughly speaking, a mid-size Indian retainer funds all of technical, all of measurement, most of content, and a deliberately narrow slice of link work. Something has to be narrow at that price. The mistake is not knowing which. Our numbers are on [the pricing page](/pricing).

faqs.q: What are the main types of SEO work?
faqs.a: Five: technical (crawling, indexing, speed, schema), content and on-page (research, writing, internal links, refreshes), off-page (links and digital PR), local (Business Profile, reviews, citations) and measurement. Most people compress this to three — on-page, off-page, technical — which hides local and measurement entirely.

Usually, but check. Some agencies scope strategy and briefs and expect you to write. Others include a fixed number of pieces. Others charge writing separately per word. All three are legitimate; only one of them is what you assumed you were buying. Get the number of pieces and the word count in writing.

faqs.q: Is link building included in SEO?
faqs.a: In a full scope, yes — eight of the roughly forty-five activities are off-page. In practice it's the first thing dropped from a cheap retainer, because real links cost real time. If a ₹25,000 monthly plan lists link building, ask how many hours it gets. The answer is usually under three.

faqs.q: How much SEO work is one-time versus ongoing?
faqs.a: About twelve activities are genuinely one-time setup: the initial crawl, redirect map, schema templates, keyword mapping, backlink audit, analytics and baseline. The remaining thirty-odd repeat on a weekly, monthly or quarterly cycle. That ratio is why SEO is priced as a retainer rather than a one-off project.

faqs.q: What should an SEO scope document actually list?
faqs.a: Activities with a cadence and an owner, not categories. "Technical SEO" is not a scope line. "Full crawl quarterly, indexation review monthly, Core Web Vitals monitored monthly, owned by the technical lead" is. If you can't tell from the document what happens in week three, it isn't a scope.

No. SEO covers organic search only. Paid search is a separate discipline with separate budgets, separate people and a completely different feedback loop. Plenty of agencies sell both — we do — but they should appear as separate line items with separate metrics, never blended into one traffic number.
